title: Criticize the Policy. Don’t Blame Your Classmate.

scenes.speaker: Maya
scenes.text: Your Jewish classmate is not a government press office.
scenes.on_screen: A CLASSMATE IS NOT A GOVERNMENT

scenes.speaker: Alex
scenes.text: Criticizing the Israeli government is not automatically antisemitic. Policies can be investigated, challenged, and protested. That’s not the same as blaming Jewish people collectively.

scenes.speaker: Maya
scenes.text: Here’s the distinction: “This policy causes harm” identifies something to examine. “You’re Jewish, so you’re responsible” assigns guilt from identity. Those are different claims.

scenes.speaker: Alex
scenes.text: You can ask anyone about their views. But being Jewish doesn’t automatically make someone answerable for another person’s decisions. And Jewish people don’t all share one political opinion.

scenes.speaker: Maya
scenes.text: The same principle protects a Palestinian classmate from being blamed for an armed group. People are responsible for their own actions, not somebody else’s label.

scenes.speaker: Alex
scenes.text: Be specific. Name the policy, the decision-maker, and the evidence. Keep the criticism attached to what happened.

scenes.speaker: Maya
scenes.text: Strong criticism needs accuracy. Not collective blame.
scenes.source: Beyond the Myth · Facts, not scapegoats
